articles.full_text:
The oil price has fallen to its lowest level in more two weeks amid new hopes of a breakthrough to end the Iran war.
Brent crude, the international benchmark, dropped by more than 6.5% to as low as $105.55 a barrel on Monday, the lowest since 16 October, sending shares in airline companies higher and pushing down government borrowing costs.
Oil prices fell after Tehran revealed that contacts between Iran and the US to end their eight-month war were continuing.
“Consultations through mediators are very intensive. We have presented our conditions and proposals and everything depends on the political rationality of Washington,” the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said, according to the state media outlet IRNA.
Over the weekend, Qatari officials tried to negotiate the release of more than $6bn (£4.5bn) in Iranian assets, so that Tehran might allow the strait of Hormuz to reopen.
On Monday, US vice-president JD Vance reported that there had been “a number of good conversations with the Iranians” and that he was feeling good about the prospects of a “negotiated settlement”.
Vance sent a letter to Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, last week but the White House has offered few details about the contents of that correspondence.
Donald Trump had earlier taken a belligerent tone, telling voters in Iowa on Sunday that Iran would receive “the hammer” unless there was progress.
“The only reason why I’m not finished with Iran is I want to be nice. I want to try and save all those lives if I can ... But at some point we’re going to have to give them the hammer,” he said during a campaign rally in the run-up to the US midterm elections.
But investors were cheered by reports on Monday that Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, had granted “powers” to his government in its talks with the US seeking to end the Middle East war.
Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “The news is manna from heaven for stock markets, which have felt increasingly pressured by oil’s rise, but of course there is still a risk that Trump will try one last throw of the iron dice after the midterms.”
The drop in the oil price sparked hopes of a break in the inflationary pressures gripping the global economy. Government borrowing costs dropped, with the yield – or interest rate – on 10-year UK bonds down 10 basis points, or 0.1 of a percentage point, to the lowest since 22 September.
Shares in British Airways’ parent company, IAG, rose by 4.2% in London, while United Airlines jumped 7% in New York.

articles.full_text:
My latest paper, The Price of a Cure: Luxturna and the Economic Dilemmas of Precision Medicine, is in the Journal of Law, Medicine and Ethics. I discuss the economics of the pharmaceutical industry and the special issues that arise with targeted drugs that cure. We are going to get many more of these drugs in the future–more value but smaller patient group–so this paper is timely.
The $850,000 price for the gene therapy Luxturna is often framed as a story of private profiteering from publicly funded science. This paper challenges that narrative. Pharmaceuticals are a hit-driven industry: most projects fail, so the few successes must earn revenues well in excess of their own direct costs if the portfolio as a whole is to attract investment. Precision medicine intensifies this logic through two core economic challenges: (1) the “sticker shock” of one-time cures, which compress decades of value into a single payment, creating a financing problem more than a value problem; and (2) the “targeting dilemma,” in which precisely targeting drugs to smaller patient groups shrinks the market, requiring higher rewards per treated patient to maintain incentives to innovate. Rather than simply controlling prices, the paper proposes a policy toolkit that includes amortizing payments over time, bundling diagnostics with drugs and insurance, and streamlining regulation to lower development costs. The aim is to preserve innovation while expanding patient access.

articles.title: Should you feel grief for the dead who go to heaven?
articles.summary:

The post Should you feel grief for the dead who go to heaven? appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.
articles.full_text:
I am not myself religious, but let us consider the possible gulf between behavior and doctrine amongst those who are.
It has long struck me as a kind of mini-puzzle why people feel so much grief for the departed, at least for the departed who are supposed to be headed for heaven (and yes there are supposed to be at least a few).
It is fine to miss those people after they are gone, but it seems that, in addition, their death is considered a tragic event to be mourned, and also if possible to be postponed.  We are crying for them, not just for ourselves.
I do not doubt the sincerity of the religious belief that these people are headed to heaven.  And I do not doubt the sincerity of the grief and mourning for their departure from this world.
So what is going on here?  Why can’t you just be happy for them?
I believe that people often construct a portfolio of moods when faced with stressful situations.  Sometimes they will mix a positive and a negative mood, other times they will mix two different kinds of negative mood (worried about a recession?  Buy a book that heralds a financial crash and hold the talisman close to your chest as pre-emptive mood management exercise.)
So if the death of a loved one is a terrible event, there is a partial assuagement if you also think they are going to heaven.  It makes their death modestly less terrible.  But if you simply celebrated their passing, you would feel disloyal and like a rotten person who cannot recognize true loss.  The point is not that you can make this bundle of feelings consistent, rather it is useful psychologically precisely because it is a portfolio and is not entirely consistent, and also not consistent over time.  As your moods change, and you need an extra dose of either modest cheer or true mourning, you can adjust your blend accordingly.
Others kinds of portfolios end up being constructed.  For instance sometimes you may focus on some other terrible thing, to distract yourself from the first pain that came along, a bit like how you might pinch yourself during a dental session.  You might prefer to have a portfolio with more pain in a way, but some of it being pain you can control.
You can multiply additional examples in these directions.
When people hold views for reasons of mood management (however sincerely), typically they are unable to respond intelligently to questions challenging their beliefs.  Even very smart people will pull b.s. out of the hat and stick with it, moving on rapidly, mentally, to some other topic.  Their response is not really thought through, it is a placeholder for “now I can move on to something else.”  After all, consistency was never the goal in the first place, you might even argue that anti-consistency was what was needed, and what proved to be psychologically stable.
I once asked someone religious about mourning death and the answer I received was something like “Well, the people in New Orleans celebrate death with funerals like parties.”  Now, I am not sure how true that is, but assume it holds.  It still resolutely refuses to address why the queried person might mourn and grieve the death of loved ones, rather than celebrate their ascent to heaven.  Nonetheless it fills in the box “I did say something back to the initial query.”  The person then wanted to simply move on to another topic.
If you challenge smart people on this issue, namely the discrepancy between beliefs and actions, they often will respond with extremely weak counters and dismissals, rather than thinking the issue through.
Once you see this kind of psychological portfolio construction in action, and learn how to identify it, you cannot unsee it.
These days, you see it especially frequently in response to AI and its advances.  People have an odd love-hate relationship with the models, and they adjust their emotional balance as their stress needs may require.  They do not want to give up either the very positive or the very negative side of their visions, because then they would have a non-diversified emotional portfolio, and they would be very vulnerable to disappointment.
You can understand some of the current AI debates by pondering how religious people react to the deaths of their loved ones.  It was never about consistency in the first place.

articles.full_text:
That is the theme of my latest Free Press article.  Excerpt, which offers the beginning of the story:
If we look at the 1960s, the John F. Kennedy and Lyndon Baines Johnson administrations brought James Tobin, Robert Solow, Kenneth Arrow (all three later Nobel laureates), Arthur Okun, Walter Heller, Gardner Ackley, Otto Eckstein, and Walt Rostow into government. Those were all names with significant academic heft who could count among the world’s leading macroeconomists. Nobel laureate Paul Samuelson served as a consultant to the government. Heller and some of the others helped to shape the Kennedy-Johnson tax cut of 1964.
That cluster of talent and its influence should come as no surprise. This was an age of elites, of love for science, of the moon landing project, and of network news shows with an establishment bent. Americans were used to deferring to elites, who had won World War II for them, and who were not out there making fools of themselves on the internet. With the Cold War raging, Americans felt their government had to get it right…
Most of this respect was still in place by the 1980s. President Ronald Reagan appointed Martin Feldstein to chair his Council of Economic Advisers (CEA), Feldstein being a Harvard professor and one of the leading market-oriented economists of his time. Two of the junior economists working for Feldstein were Paul Krugman and Lawrence Summers—before they became famous, but the intellectual firepower was already there. Michael Mussa and William Niskanen were other notables in the administration, and Milton Friedman and Friedrich A. Hayek were standing sources of inspiration.
And this:
On top of those political trends, there are further mechanisms at work pushing down the social status of economists. The Trump administration is proposing to eliminate social sciences funding at the National Science Foundation, and there are declining enrollments on the horizon for American colleges and universities. Academia is now seen as more politicized and left-leaning than used to be the case. Our best AI models are often better economists than the humans, just as they are proving theorems that human mathematicians cannot. All of those trends, even if you might consider some of them good news overall, are reinforcing a declining status for economists.
Worth a ponder.

articles.full_text:
Both of these movies I found worth watching.  Fjord won the Golden Prize at Cannes, and it concerns the rights of the family vs. the rights of the state, when it comes to raising children.  As I interpreted the story, it was so right-wing and so based I am shocked it won.  It is by the Romanian director Cristian Mungiu, who is best known for 4 Months, 3 Weeks, and 2 Days, also referred to as “the Romanian abortion movie.”  His new outing is a quality film but I found theh messaging a bit heavy-handed at times (and am I one to defend European bureaucracy?), noting that some critics are still debating which side the director took so “maybe it is just me.”
Fatherland is a Polish take on postwar Germany and some travels of Thomas Mann and his daughter Erika.  A German director might have been afraid to portray the communism of East Germany as this movie does, in any case I found that convincing.  It captures what I imagine the immediate postwar era to have been like, and the moral dilemmas people faced as they had to decide their future relationships with Germany (and indeed Germanies), past, present, and future.  At one hour, twenty-two minutes it worked very well, though it requires the viewer to know a good deal about German history, literature, and culture.

articles.title: Texas voters on high gas prices under Trump: ‘Probably made me go more Democrat’
articles.summary: In state where driving is part of life, president’s pledge to lower prices at the pumps cuts little iceBehind the granite countertops of Fuel City, a gas station in Dallas where taxidermy deer flank the entrance and hot tacos are served 24/7, Alina Cardenas sees first-hand that Texans are stretched thin.Drivers are filling up less, she said, while ringing people up for cigarettes and beer, and fewer people are buying a full tank. articles.full_text:
Behind the granite countertops of Fuel City, a gas station in Dallas where taxidermy deer flank the entrance and hot tacos are served 24/7, Alina Cardenas sees first-hand that Texans are stretched thin.
Drivers are filling up less, she said, while ringing people up for cigarettes and beer, and fewer people are buying a full tank. Some stop once they’ve reached $10 or $20 worth of gasoline.
Cardenas, 19, who is studying radiology at a local college, said she’s been cutting back on gas herself by staying home more and driving only to go to work and school.
“It’s just getting really expensive,” she said. “Things got harder this year.”
In a state nearly three times the size of the UK, with hundreds of thousands of miles of road, driving is an essential part of life. Commuters can spend as much as six hours a day on the road going to and from their jobs. Over much of the past year, soaring energy costs brought on by the war in Iran has made it all the more expensive.
Higher gas prices are expected to play a major role in how Texas voters will decide a key battle in the upcoming midterms. James Talarico, a state representative, is trying to best Republican Ken Paxton, a former state attorney general, to become the state’s first Democratic senator in over 30 years.
Republicans across the country are fighting an uphill battle against widespread frustration, especially among independent voters, over the economy. Recent polling shows Talarico with a slight edge over Paxton, who has been embroiled in scandals.
On Tuesday, a week before election day, Donald Trump stood in front of an oil tanker docked in Corpus Christi, Texas to announce that the first million barrels of oil from his deal with Venezuela had arrived in the state.
“We’re celebrating the greatest oil victory in history,” Trump said at a rally for Paxton in Lubbock later that day.
At another rally in Georgia later in the week, Trump touted the “hundreds of billions of dollars” that higher gas prices are bringing to American gas companies. Two of the largest, Exxon and Chevron, are based in Texas.
“We’re making a frickin’ fortune,” he told the crowd.
But in Texas, voters seem unconvinced. In the Dallas-Fort Worth area, where bumper stickers declaring “my country, not your church” speed past billboards for gun shows, drivers who spoke to the Guardian expressed deep frustration over gas prices.
Cardenas said inflated gas prices has “probably made me go more Democrat” and that she will vote for Talarico.
Tom L, 40, who declined to give his last name, said he commutes nearly six hours each day to get to his job as a data analyst in Dallas. He spends about $400 a month on gas, double what he was spending a year ago. The diesel truck that he uses for farm work now costs him around $200 a week.
“I’ve definitely had to budget tighter to compensate,” he said.
He voted for Trump in the 2024 presidential election, but said he is “not sure if that was the right decision” and is unsure which Senate candidate he will support as both have their benefits and flaws.
Because Texas is a top oil producer, its residents often enjoy cheaper gas prices than the rest of the US. But the state has not been immune to the rising cost of gas amid the war in Iran. On average, a gallon of gas now costs $3.68, compared to $2.59 a year ago, according to AAA.
Diesel, which fuels the big rigs and tanker trucks that transport Texan oil, has shot up by more than 80%, from $3.18 to $5.79.
“Texans are paying less than the national average, yes, but they are also paying a lot more than they were a year ago,” said Tom Seng, a professor of energy finances at Texas Christian University. “Texans are feeling the pain just like everyone else.”
Though gas prices are just part of a slate of costs that make up everyday expenses, they tend to be the most noticeable, especially in a state where residents heavily rely on their cars for transportation.
“People on Tuesday morning, before they go to the polls … they’re not opening up their electric utility bill. They probably aren’t grocery shopping that morning,” Seng said. “But what’s the last thing that they’re probably going to see before they get to the polling place? The price of gasoline.”
Kobe Montgomery, a security guard at Fuel City in Dallas, said he uses his car to get to his job in security and to deliver for UberEats and Domino’s on the side. He has no choice but to fill up his tank whenever he needs to.
“It beats walking,” he said.
But even though he hasn’t noticed the higher cost of gas, he doesn’t plan to vote at all in the upcoming midterms, out of fear for voting for the wrong person and regretting it.
Diamond M, who declined to give her last name, said spends at least three hours on the road to get to her job as a warehouse worker. Gas, she estimates, is taking up about 20% of her take-home pay. She only fills up her tank on Friday – pay day –and forces herself to make the tank stretch the whole week.
She plans to vote for Talarico, who she believes has the best shot of lowering costs for her.
“He has a voice,” she said. “Seems like he’ll get it done.”

articles.title: ‘The content creator election’: digital streamers and TV networks face off for midterms coverage
articles.summary: Journalists such as Jim Acosta and Scott MacFarlane are now competing against their former employers for eyeballsOn Tuesday, for the first time in more than 20 years, Jim Acosta, a former CNN stalwart, will not be working for a mainstream television network on election night.Acosta, who left CNN last year after nearly 18 years at the network, is putting on his own live broadcast at the University of Virginia that will air on YouTube and his Substack platform. articles.full_text:
On Tuesday, for the first time in more than 20 years, Jim Acosta, a former CNN stalwart, will not be working for a mainstream television network on election night.
Acosta, who left CNN last year after nearly 18 years at the network, is putting on his own live broadcast at the University of Virginia that will air on YouTube and his Substack platform.
And in a sign of the times, Acosta will be joined for the broadcast, hosted by the university’s Center for Politics, by another star of linear television – Katie Couric, a former Today show co-host. (Don Lemon, another CNN alum and converted new media player, may also drop by, Acosta said.)
“If folks are looking for fresh faces and a different way of doing this kind of coverage, I think it’s going to deliver that,” Acosta said.
Acosta said he will be doing his best Steve Kornacki impression, giving analysis using an interactive, touch screen battleground map just like the NBC News data guru. “Yeah, I’m going to have to go to J Crew and get some new khakis.”
Rashida Jones, who serves as chief executive of Piers Morgan’s media company Uncensored, predicted that Tuesday’s midterms will come to be remembered as “the content creator election”, when independent journalists hosting streaming broadcasts give traditional networks a run for their money.
Jones was running one of those television networks, MSNBC (now called MS Now), during the 2024 presidential election, a role she held for four years. She is working to expand Morgan’s company by launching new shows and verticals beyond the “Piers Morgan Uncensored” streaming broadcast, which has about 4.5 million subscribers on YouTube.
The plan for election night is a several-hour-long live show hosted by Morgan from Washington DC, part of a three-day stint broadcasting from the US capital city.
“Our focus is going to be making sense of what’s happening in real time,” she said in an interview. “People aren’t coming to us because they’re looking for how this part of Michigan voted. It’s more the big picture themes and takeaways. Ultimately by the end of the night, people care about where did we land, less about the individual races.”
Jones said that traditional television networks will be facing more competition than past election cycles. “If I’m a network that’s got a guy at a board and a ticker at the bottom, and I just assume people are going to come, I don’t know that that’s baked in and that’s a given this cycle. And I think what we see [on Tuesday] will be on a smaller scale what we see for the general election … I think it’ll be the content creator election.”
Scott MacFarlane, a veteran reporter who resigned from CBS News in March seeking “some independence”, joined the progressive MeidasTouch network as its chief Washington correspondent and will be co-hosting its live election broadcast.
MacFarlane says the streaming show will lack the bells and whistles of a traditional television election broadcast, which is the point. “There will be no teleprompters and no scripts,” he said. “It’s straight to the point, direct, conversational and heavy on original reporting.” He added that “dramatic theme music and theatrical presentations would miss the moment”.
Still, many millions of Americans will be watching a traditional television network – or their streaming off-shoot – to keep tabs on the elections. On election night 2024, an estimated 42.3 million viewers watched television coverage – though viewership is obviously lower for non-presidential years.
“There are more places than ever for people to get their news and information, but there’s no place that has the depth, the scope, and the breadth that NBC News has,” said Hallie Jackson, an NBC News anchor, who is penciled in for nine hours of live coverage as part of the network’s election team, along with Savannah Guthrie, Tom Llamas and Kristen Welker behind the desk (along with Kornacki).
Jackson said the key to election night is hydration, and a regimen of healthy eating that she began last week. “You have to pace yourself. You have to stay hydrated. You have to have a secret pack of M&Ms for your blood sugar that you can come back to every hour.”
Seni Tienabeso, vice-president of ABC News Live and Specialized Units, said the network has planned for a seven-hour-long broadcast, but could go much longer if a key call – perhaps for control of the US Senate or House – is on the horizon.
Asked how much effort is put toward the traditional television broadcast compared with digital and social media offerings, ABC News executives said the network is fully integrated. “For us, it’s about reaching the audience where they are,” Tienabeso said. “We don’t leave any of those arenas as secondary.” (The network’s coverage will also be aired on its ABC News Live digital channel, on Hulu, and on the Disney+ streaming service.)
Like most major networks and news organizations, ABC News relies on election results from the Associated Press – as well as a new voter survey conducted by the polling firm SSRS – to help make projections about key elections. Those decisions are made by a desk that is “holed off” from the rest of the newsroom, Tienabeso said, and is not primarily focused on beating rival networks. “We don’t pay attention to what competitors are doing,” he said. “Our decision desk makes the decision when they feel comfortable with their analysis of the race that they’re covering.”
On Tuesday, viewers watching CNN will be able to see the network’s decision desk in action, and will also have access to a new tool called CNN Sightline that will give insights into how a contest is leaning, based on both data and demographics. “I think it’s probably more transparency than we’ve ever had,” said David Chalian, CNN’s political director and Washington bureau chief.
CNN’s decision desk makes calls when they have at least 99.5% confidence that a certain candidate will win. “Speed is not part of that at all,” he said.
“In a time when voter confidence in elections is something that we constantly look at and is called into question, it only ups the seriousness of purpose with which we take this mission in projecting races,” Chalian added.
Chris Stirewalt, who serves as political editor for the cable network NewsNation and anchors the weekly show The Hill Sunday, said he doesn’t think that Republicans will be happy with the election results. He said that early returns from Ohio will be a good indication of whether “the rout is on” for Democrats.
Stirewalt is no stranger to election night, having been part of Fox News’ decision desk for several cycles before leaving the network in 2021. He said he values the finality of the process: “The conversation goes on and on and on, and then it’s over. And you count, look at the scoreboard, and then it’s done. I love that.”
While Acosta is best-known for his television work, he said he doesn’t miss CNN and is happy to be “starting something at the beginning” by working in creator-driven media. “And that’s kind of the exciting part of it, because who knows where this thing is going to take us?”
